title: One chemical mixture keeps switching colour back and forth on its own

cover.alt: A glass beaker of pale peach-coloured liquid sits on a metal stand in front of a green chalkboard.

body: Most chemical reactions run one way and then stop changing. The **Belousov–Zhabotinsky reaction** is different: a bromate, an organic acid such as malonic acid and a metal catalyst, all in dilute sulfuric acid, keep cycling between two sets of reactions, one making bromine and the other using it up again. Because the mixture stays far from equilibrium, its colour swings back and forth, here between colourless and orange-brown with a manganese catalyst, until the reagents run out. Boris Belousov stumbled on it in 1951 while looking for a chemical version of the Krebs cycle, the chain of reactions cells use to release energy.

slides.alt: A beaker of liquid on a stand turns from pale peach to deep orange-brown, fades back to almost colourless, then flashes orange-brown again, several times over.
slides.caption: With manganese as the catalyst, the mixture flips between colourless and orange-brown again and again. The film-makers sped up their footage.

left.label: Most reactions
left.text: They run towards equilibrium, a balance point, and once they get there nothing visible changes any more.

right.label: This one
right.text: It stays far from equilibrium for a long time, so its chemistry keeps swinging back and forth until the reagents are used up.

slides.heading: Seventeen years to reach the West
slides.note: Belousov saw a cerium catalyst oscillate; the 1968 meeting brought the reaction to the West

slides.prompt: Spread the mixture in a thin layer in a dish and it doesn’t just flash on and off. What appears?
slides.answer: Expanding rings and spirals of colour
slides.detail: Coloured spots form first and grow into rings or spirals. Shake the dish and they vanish, then come back, until the reagents run out.

slides.question: Why did journals turn down Belousov’s paper?
slides.explanation: Twice his paper was rejected because he could not explain the results to the editors’ satisfaction. In 1959 it finally appeared in a journal that did not review papers.
